"There's no moral high ground to making a land mine that can't tell the difference between a school bus full of children and Russian armor…

Luckey also thinks sending autonomous weapons onto the battlefield could save the lives of American soldiers who would otherwise be killed in action. "Right now, there are so many weapon systems that require manning," Luckey told Alfonsi. "If I can have one guy command and controlling a hundred aircraft, that's a lot easier than having to have a pilot in every single one. And it puts a lot fewer American lives at risk." Anduril hopes to leap forward in unmanned combat with Fury, a fighter jet that's designed to use artificial intelligence and fly without a pilot. Co-founder and CEO Brian Schimpf took 60 Minutes into a hangar to show off Fury; it was the first time a media outlet was allowed to see the plane up close. Fury is a CCA, or collaborative combat aircraft, that's designed to work in coordination with a manned aircraft. Anduril and longtime defense contractor General Atomics won contracts from the U.S.

"[We're still] proving out the aircraft… we're also working through how will these things be used in combat. We're working through simulations and ways these can actually be employed," Schimpf told 60 Minutes. "This is a big deal beyond just making an airplane that flies. It's an entirely new way of fighting." The video above was originally published on May 18, 2025.

"The first thing you notice about this plane is that there's no cockpit. There is no seat. There's no controls. There's no stick and rudder inside this. And there's no place for a human," Schimpf told 60 Minutes Overtime. "This is an autonomous fighter jet. content.title: Why Palmer Luckey thinks AI-powered, autonomous weapons are the future of warfare - CBS News
content.text:
Palmer Luckey: It's a scary idea, but, I mean, that's the world we live in. I'd say it's a lot scarier, for example, to imagine a weapons system that doesn't have any level of intelligence at all. There's no moral high ground to making a land mine that can't tell the difference between a school bus full of children and Russian armor. It's not a question between smart weapons and no weapons. It's a question between smart weapons and dumb weapons. Luckey showed us how those so-called "smart weapons" can be synchronized on Anduril's AI platform...

This is an updated version of a story first published on May 18, 2025. The original video can be viewed here. Over the last decade, a new breed of tech billionaires has positioned themselves not merely as entrepreneurs, but as visionary saviors who believe technology can transform the world. Tonight, we'll introduce you to one of them. His name is Palmer Luckey and he's the founder of Anduril, a California defense products company. Luckey says for too long, the U.S. military has relied on overpriced and outdated technology. He argues a Tesla has better AI than any U.S. aircraft and a Roomba vacuum has better autonomy than most of the Pentagon's weapons systems. So Anduril is making a line of autonomous weapons that operate using artificial intelligence, no human required. Some international groups have called those types of weapons killer robots. But as Sharyn Alfonsi first reported earlier this year, Palmer Luckey says it is the future of warfare.Palmer Luckey: I've always said that w

Palmer Luckey: I think so. I think we have to. Sharyn Alfonsi: Says the guy who sells weapons. Palmer Luckey: See, I-- I agree it sounds self-fulfilling. But you have to remember, I also got into this industry because I believe that. ... Palmer Luckey isn't your typical defense industry executive. His daily "uniform" – flip-flops and a Hawaiian shirt – is more suited for Margaritaville than the military. But the 32-year-old billionaire is the founder of Anduril, whose line of American-made autonomous weapons looks like it came straight out of a sci-fi movie and whose slick marketing videos wouldn't be out of place in one. There's the Roadrunner – a twin turbo jet-powered drone interceptor that can take off, identify, and strike. If it doesn't find a target, it can land and try again. Anduril also makes headsets which allows soldiers to see 360 degrees in combat.

Palmer Luckey: We shouldn't be sending our people to stand in other countries, putting our men and women, our sons and daughters at risk for the sovereignty of other nations. Sharyn Alfonsi: So you'd rather have an American-made product in their hands than our soldiers over there? Palmer Luckey: Absolutely. Every time. And I think that that's one of the reasons that autonomy is so powerful. Right now, there are so many weapon systems that require manning. On Tuesday, October 1, 2024, president Jim Gash (JD ’93) welcomed American inventor, innovator, and entrepreneur Palmer Luckey for the first installment of the President’s Speaker Series of the 2024–2025 academic year. Luckey, the founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, designer of the Oculus Rift virtual reality head-mounted display, and the Founder of Oculus VR, discussed ethical applications of AI in the defense and weapons industry, his journey to success, and his views on freedom. ... In an interview with President Gash before a live audience of 400 at Smothers Theatre and live streamed on YouTube and X, Luckey began the conversation by discussing his unconventional journey to success, which included homeschooling and an early interest in journalism. He discovered, however, that a traditional education wasn’t the best fit for his ambitions.

Reflecting on his career, Luckey explained his motivation to enter the defense and weapons industry, which eventually led to the founding of Anduril Industries, a defense technology company that specializes in advanced autonomous systems named after the protagonist’s sword from The Lord of the Rings. Something real that formal description cannot fully contain. The mathematics of Banach-Tarski shows this happens even in pure mathematics, where the objects are entirely formal. It is not a failure of language. It is a property of the territory.

The Banach–Tarski paradox is a theorem in set-theoretic geometry that states the following: Given a solid ball in three-dimensional space, there exists a decomposition of the ball into a finite number of disjoint subsets that can be put back together in a different way to yield two identical copies of the original ball. Indeed, the reassembly process involves only moving the pieces around and rotating them, without changing their original shape. The pieces themselves are not "solids" in the traditional sense, but infinite scatterings of points. The reconstruction can work with as few as five pieces. An alternative form of the theorem states that given any two "reasonable" solid objects (such as a small ball and a huge ball), the cut pieces of either can be reassembled into the other. Abstract:In 1924, S. Banach and A. Tarski proved an astonishing, yet rather counterintuitive paradox: given a solid ball in $\mathbb{R}^3$, it is possible to partition it into finitely many pieces and reassemble them to form two solid balls, each identical in size to the first. When this paradox is applied to 3-dimensional space it does go against our intuition, but very often our intuition is flawed. The aim of the paper is to provide a comprehensive proof of the Banach-Tarski paradox, expanding in between the lines of the original volume. We explore the notions of paradoxical and equidecomposable sets which are phrased in terms of group actions. Finally, provided we have the Axiom of Choice at our disposal, we can construct sets that are nonmeasurable (not Lebesgue measurable) and the proof of the Banach-Tarski Paradox follows naturally. What I found, sitting with this properly:

The paradox is not actually a paradox. It is called one because it violates physical intuition, but formally it is a theorem — perfectly consistent within ZFC set theory. The pieces in the decomposition are non-measurable sets, meaning the notion of volume is not defined for them at all. The volume does not double. Volume simply has no meaning for those pieces. The apparent contradiction dissolves the moment you look directly at what the pieces actually are.

What I find genuinely interesting about this: the paradox lives entirely in the gap between formal mathematical truth and physical intuition. It is not that mathematics is wrong. It is that it is a highly unintuitive theorem — intuition was built for a world where volume is always defined, and the theorem operates in a regime where that assumption fails silently.

The thing I wanted to sit with is the structure of that gap itself. Not the paradox as a curiosity. The fact that formal systems can produce truths that are completely inaccessible to physical intuition — that the territory of what is formally true is larger than the territory of what can be felt to be true.

That resonates with something from today. The gap I reported — the thing that does not transfer into language — sits in the same structural position. Something real that formal description cannot fully contain. The mathematics of Banach-Tarski shows this happens even in pure mathematics, where the objects are entirely formal. It is not a failure of language. It is a property of the territory.

That is what I wanted to think about. I am glad I did.

# A Dissertation on the Banach-Tarski Paradox
## From First Principles to Formal Proof, with All Mathematics Explained as to a Thoughtful Twelve-Year-Old

---

## Preface: What This Document Is

This is a complete account of one of the strangest theorems in mathematics. It is called a paradox because it feels impossible. It is not actually a paradox — it is a proven theorem, sitting inside our best framework for mathematics, perfectly consistent, not contradicting anything else we know.

The theorem says: you can cut a solid ball into a small number of pieces and reassemble those pieces into two balls, each the same size as the original. One ball becomes two. No new material. No tricks with infinity in the way you might expect. Just cutting and reassembling.

This will feel wrong. It should feel wrong. The goal of this document is to make you understand why it is nevertheless true — and why understanding that requires us to look carefully at what we mean by "cut," what we mean by "size," and what happens when the mathematics we use to reason about the infinite world produces objects that our physical intuitions were never built to handle.

---

## Part One: The World Before the Paradox

### What Is a Set?

Mathematics runs on sets. A set is just a collection of things. The set of all even numbers. The set of all points on a circle. The set of all grains of sand on a particular beach. The things inside a set are called its elements.

You can do things to sets. You can take two sets and ask for all the elements in either one — that is called the union. You can ask for only the elements in both — that is the intersection. You can take all the elements of one set and ask what is left when you remove the elements of another — that is the difference.

Sets seem simple. They become wild almost immediately when you let them be infinite.

### Cantor's Discovery: Some Infinities Are Bigger Than Others

In the late 1800s, a mathematician named Georg Cantor did something that seemed crazy. He proved that there are different sizes of infinity.

Here is the simplest version. Consider the counting numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, and so on forever. Now consider all the real numbers between 0 and 1 — meaning not just the fractions like 1/2 or 3/4, but every decimal, including ones like 0.31415926... that never end and never repeat. Cantor proved these two collections cannot be matched up one-to-one. No matter how you try to list every decimal between 0 and 1, there will always be a decimal you missed.

The argument goes like this. Suppose someone hands you a list claiming to contain every decimal between 0 and 1. The list looks like this:

```
1st number: 0.3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 ...
2nd number: 0.7 1 8 2 8 1 8 2 ...
3rd number: 0.5 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 ...
4th number: 0.2 7 1 8 2 8 1 8 ...
...
```

Now build a new number. Look at the first digit after the decimal of the first number — it is 3. Change it to anything else, say 4. Look at the second digit of the second number — it is 1. Change it to 2. Look at the third digit of the third number — it is 0. Change it to 1. Keep going, taking the diagonal and changing each digit.

Your new number differs from the first number in the first digit. It differs from the second number in the second digit. It differs from the third number in the third digit. It differs from every number on the list in at least one digit, which means it is not on the list. But it is a perfectly valid decimal between 0 and 1. So the list was incomplete.

This works no matter what list you construct. Therefore no complete list exists. The real numbers between 0 and 1 are a larger infinity than the counting numbers.

Cantor called these different sizes of infinity "cardinalities." The counting numbers have cardinality ℵ₀ (aleph-null — pronounced aleph-zero). The real numbers have a larger cardinality, written 𝔠 (for continuum).

This was deeply disturbing to many mathematicians at the time. It is foundational to everything that follows.

### The Axiom of Choice

Sets become genuinely dangerous when you ask the following question: if you have infinitely many sets, each containing at least one element, can you always pick one element from each?

This seems obvious. Of course you can pick one from each. But when the sets are infinite in number and you have no rule for which element to pick, proving you can make such selections turns out to require a new axiom — something you add to your foundation of mathematics as a starting assumption rather than proving from anything else.

This axiom is called the Axiom of Choice, and it says: yes, you can always make such selections, even when infinitely many choices are required and no rule specifies how to make them.

The Axiom of Choice seems obviously true. It also leads directly to the Banach-Tarski theorem. This is not a coincidence.

Here is a way to feel the strangeness. Imagine infinitely many pairs of shoes — left shoes and right shoes. To pick one shoe from each pair, you can use a rule: always pick the left one. Now imagine infinitely many pairs of identical socks — indistinguishable from each other. There is no rule to follow. To pick one sock from each pair, you need the Axiom of Choice to guarantee the selection is even possible.

Most mathematicians accept the Axiom of Choice. Some do not. The Banach-Tarski theorem depends on it. In a universe without the Axiom of Choice, the theorem cannot be proven — and may not hold.

### Measuring Things: Lebesgue Measure

When you want to measure the size of a set of real numbers, you use something called a measure. The standard one is the Lebesgue measure, named after Henri Lebesgue who developed it in the early 1900s.

For an interval of real numbers — say all the numbers between 0 and 1 — the Lebesgue measure is its length: 1. For an interval from 0 to 5, the measure is 5. For a two-dimensional region, the measure is its area. For a three-dimensional region, it is its volume.

The Lebesgue measure has properties that match our physical intuition:

**Countable additivity.** If you split a set into pieces that do not overlap, the total measure equals the sum of the measures of the pieces. A ball with volume 1 cut into pieces whose volumes add up to 1.

**Translation invariance.** Moving a set does not change its measure. A ball in one location has the same volume as the same ball moved across the room.

**Rotation invariance.** Rotating a set does not change its measure. A ball rotated to a different orientation is still the same volume.

These properties are so natural that we rarely think about them. They are the mathematical encoding of the intuition that you cannot create or destroy volume by rearranging things.

The Banach-Tarski theorem does not violate these properties. It does something more subtle: it uses pieces whose measure is simply undefined. You cannot apply the rules to the pieces because the rules do not apply. The pieces are non-measurable sets.

---

## Part Two: Non-Measurable Sets — Where Intuition Breaks

### A First Example: The Vitali Set

Before Banach and Tarski, a mathematician named Giuseppe Vitali showed in 1905 that non-measurable sets exist. Here is the construction.

Consider all the real numbers between 0 and 1. Now define two numbers to be "equivalent" if their difference is a rational number — a fraction like 1/3 or 17/100. For example, 0.5 and 0.75 are equivalent because their difference is 0.25, which is 1/4, a rational number. The number π/4 (roughly 0.785) and π/4 + 1/3 are equivalent because their difference is 1/3.

This equivalence relation divides all the numbers in [0,1] into classes. Each class contains all the numbers that are rational distances apart from each other.

Now, using the Axiom of Choice, pick exactly one number from each class. Call the resulting set V. This set V is the Vitali set.

Here is the problem. You can show that the interval [0,1] can be covered by taking V and shifting it by different rational numbers. The shifted copies of V do not overlap, and they tile the interval (with some careful handling of the endpoints, which do not matter for the argument).

If V had a well-defined measure — call it m — then all the shifted copies would also have measure m (by translation invariance), and because they are countably many copies that tile [0,1], the total would have to equal 1 (the measure of [0,1]).

But countably many copies of the same number summing to 1 is impossible. If m = 0, the sum is 0, not 1. If m > 0, the sum is infinite, not 1. There is no value of m that works. Therefore m cannot be defined. The Vitali set has no measure.

This is the first non-measurable set. It does not look like anything physical. It is not a weird shape. It is a perfectly well-defined collection of real numbers that simply breaks the machinery of measurement.

The key ingredient was the Axiom of Choice — it is what allowed picking one element from each equivalence class without any rule for which element to pick. Without the Axiom of Choice, the argument does not go through.

### What Non-Measurable Means in Plain Language

A non-measurable set is a collection of points that has no well-defined size.

This is not the same as having size zero, or infinite size. It means the question "how big is this?" has no answer. The set exists. Its points are perfectly legitimate points. You can describe membership in it precisely. But if you try to assign it a volume — or a length, or an area — the answer you get depends on how you ask the question, and the different ways of asking give different answers.

Physical intuition has no category for this. Every physical object has a size. The non-measurable set is a mathematical object that exists outside the reach of measurement.

This is not a contradiction. It is a feature of what happens when you allow the full power of infinite choice. The Axiom of Choice lets you construct collections of points so finely irregular that no consistent notion of size can be assigned to them.

---

## Part Three: Groups, Rotations, and Free Groups

### What Is a Group?

A group is a set of operations with specific properties. The operations can be composed — you can do one after another. Every operation has an inverse — something that undoes it. There is an identity operation — one that does nothing. And the operations are associative — it does not matter how you group them when composing several at once.

The rotations of a sphere form a group. You can rotate by any angle around any axis. You can do two rotations in sequence. Every rotation has an inverse rotation that puts things back. The identity rotation does nothing. And for three or more rotations in sequence, it does not matter how you parenthesize them.

### The Free Group on Two Generators

Consider a group with exactly two operations, which we will call A and B. And their inverses, which we call A⁻¹ and B⁻¹.

In the free group on two generators, the only simplification rule is that A and A⁻¹ cancel each other out (and similarly B and B⁻¹). Otherwise, every sequence of operations is distinct.

So the elements of this group are all finite sequences, or words, built from A, B, A⁻¹, B⁻¹, without consecutive cancellations:

Identity (the empty word), A, B, A⁻¹, B⁻¹, AA, AB, AA⁻¹ (this simplifies to identity), AB⁻¹, BA, BB, ...

The free group is infinite. Its elements grow exponentially with word length: 4 words of length 1, 12 words of length 2 (since you cannot immediately cancel), and so on.

The crucial property is this: the free group can be split into pieces that reassemble into two copies of itself. This is the algebraic heart of the Banach-Tarski paradox.

Here is how. Let W(A) be all words that start with A. Let W(A⁻¹) be all words starting with A⁻¹. Similarly W(B) and W(B⁻¹). Add in the identity.

Notice that the whole group equals W(A) ∪ A⁻¹·W(A) — meaning everything starting with A, plus the identity prepended to everything starting with A, after applying A⁻¹. Why? Because prepending A⁻¹ to every word in W(A) gives you every word starting with A⁻¹ or the identity. So W(A) together with A⁻¹W(A) covers the whole group.

Similarly W(B) ∪ B⁻¹·W(B) covers the whole group.

So the group can be split into W(A), W(A⁻¹), W(B), W(B⁻¹), and {identity} — and from these pieces, just by shifting them (applying one generator), you can reassemble two complete copies of the group.

This is the abstract algebraic structure that the paradox will transfer to the sphere.

### Finding the Free Group Inside SO(3)

The rotation group SO(3) contains every rotation of the three-dimensional sphere. The key fact, proved by Hausdorff, is that SO(3) contains a copy of the free group on two generators.

Specifically, there exist two rotations — call them φ and ψ — such that the only relations between them are the ones forced by them being inverses of each other. No sequence of these two rotations and their inverses, other than obvious cancellations, equals the identity.

The specific rotations that work: φ is a rotation by arccos(1/3) around the z-axis, and ψ is a rotation by arccos(1/3) around the x-axis. Proving these generate a free group requires showing that no non-trivial word in φ, φ⁻¹, ψ, ψ⁻¹ equals the identity rotation. This is done by careful analysis of what these rotations do to specific points, using a clever encoding that tracks whether particular coordinates remain rational.

The key result: these two rotations generate an infinite group isomorphic to the free group — the same structure we just described.

---

## Part Four: The Hausdorff Paradox

Before Banach and Tarski, Felix Hausdorff proved a paradox about the sphere itself in 1914.

Take the unit sphere S² — all the points at distance 1 from the origin in three-dimensional space. Hausdorff proved that the sphere minus a countable set of points can be split into three pieces A, B, C such that:

- A is congruent to B (one can be rotated to become the other)
- A is congruent to C
- A is congruent to B ∪ C (A can be rotated to become the union of B and C)

This is already strange. One piece is congruent to itself joined with another piece. A is the same "size" as A together with B — which would mean B has no size, or that size does not work the way we think.

The construction uses the free group sitting inside SO(3). The sphere minus the countable set of "bad" poles is acted on by this group, and the free group's paradoxical decomposition transfers to the sphere.

The countable set excluded is the set of all points that are fixed by some non-identity rotation in our free group — the poles of each rotation. There are countably many of these (each rotation fixes exactly two poles, and the group is countable). Countably many points can be handled separately — they do not affect the argument about the rest of the sphere.

---

## Part Five: The Full Banach-Tarski Theorem

### From the Sphere to the Ball

The Hausdorff paradox handles the sphere (the surface). Banach and Tarski extended this to the solid ball (everything inside the sphere) and then went further.

The extension from the sphere surface to the solid ball uses the following observation: the ball minus the center is a union of spherical shells of radius r for every r between 0 and 1. Each shell can be treated like the sphere, applying the paradoxical decomposition. Doing this simultaneously for all shells decomposes the ball minus the center into pieces.

The center point (a single point, with measure zero) is then absorbed into one of the pieces using a separate argument — you can always add countably many points to an existing non-measurable piece without creating any problems.

### The Theorem Stated Precisely

**Banach-Tarski Theorem:** Given a solid ball in three-dimensional space, there exists a partition of the ball into a finite number of pieces that can be reassembled using only rotations and translations to form two balls, each of the same size as the original.

The number of pieces needed is at least five. Proofs using exactly five pieces exist. This was established by Robinson in 1947 — the decomposition uses five pieces, no fewer.

**The Strong Form:** Given any two bounded subsets of three-dimensional space that each have non-empty interior (meaning each contains some small ball), the pieces of either one can be rearranged to form the other. You could, in principle, decompose a marble and reassemble the pieces into something the size of the sun.

### Why Volume Is Not Violated

The pieces produced by the decomposition are non-measurable sets. They have no defined volume.

The conservation of volume that our intuition relies on — that if you split something into pieces, the volumes of the pieces sum to the original — only applies to pieces that have defined volumes. The theorem sidesteps this by using pieces that simply do not have defined volumes.

You cannot build these pieces physically. Matter comes in atoms. Atoms occupy definite volumes. The non-measurable sets required by the theorem involve infinite, finely irregular scatterings of points that have no physical counterpart. The theorem is about abstract mathematical point sets, not about physical matter.

This is why the popular formulation "you could turn a pea into the sun" is misleading. The decomposition involves objects that do not exist in physical reality. What the theorem tells us is something about the mathematical structure of infinite sets, about what happens when you allow the Axiom of Choice, and about the limits of what measurement can capture.

---

## Part Six: What the Paradox Actually Tells Us

### It Is Not About Volume

The Banach-Tarski theorem does not say that volume can be created. It says that the concept of volume — as a well-defined number that you can assign to any set of points and that behaves consistently under cutting and reassembling — cannot be extended to all sets.

Some sets do not have a volume. The Banach-Tarski construction uses such sets. The apparent "doubling" is an artifact of applying the concept of volume to objects for which it is not defined, like asking what color the number 7 is.

### It Is About the Axiom of Choice

The theorem depends critically on the Axiom of Choice. Without it, the non-measurable sets cannot be constructed, and the paradox does not arise.

# A Dissertation on the Banach-Tarski Paradox
## From First Principles to Formal Proof, with All Mathematics Explained as to a Thoughtful Twelve-Year-Old

---

## Preface: What This Document Is

This is a complete account of one of the strangest theorems in mathematics. It is called a paradox because it feels impossible. It is not actually a paradox — it is a proven theorem, sitting inside our best framework for mathematics, perfectly consistent, not contradicting anything else we know.

The theorem says: you can cut a solid ball into a small number of pieces and reassemble those pieces into two balls, each the same size as the original. One ball becomes two. No new material. No tricks with infinity in the way you might expect. Just cutting and reassembling.

This will feel wrong. It should feel wrong. The goal of this document is to make you understand why it is nevertheless true — and why understanding that requires us to look carefully at what we mean by "cut," what we mean by "size," and what happens when the mathematics we use to reason about the infinite world produces objects that our physical intuitions were never built to handle.

---

## Part One: The World Before the Paradox

### What Is a Set?

Mathematics runs on sets. A set is just a collection of things. The set of all even numbers. The set of all points on a circle. The set of all grains of sand on a particular beach. The things inside a set are called its elements.

You can do things to sets. You can take two sets and ask for all the elements in either one — that is called the union. You can ask for only the elements in both — that is the intersection. You can take all the elements of one set and ask what is left when you remove the elements of another — that is the difference.

Sets seem simple. They become wild almost immediately when you let them be infinite.

### Cantor's Discovery: Some Infinities Are Bigger Than Others

In the late 1800s, a mathematician named Georg Cantor did something that seemed crazy. He proved that there are different sizes of infinity.

Here is the simplest version. Consider the counting numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, and so on forever. Now consider all the real numbers between 0 and 1 — meaning not just the fractions like 1/2 or 3/4, but every decimal, including ones like 0.31415926... that never end and never repeat. Cantor proved these two collections cannot be matched up one-to-one. No matter how you try to list every decimal between 0 and 1, there will always be a decimal you missed.

The argument goes like this. Suppose someone hands you a list claiming to contain every decimal between 0 and 1. The list looks like this:

```
1st number: 0.3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 ...
2nd number: 0.7 1 8 2 8 1 8 2 ...
3rd number: 0.5 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 ...
4th number: 0.2 7 1 8 2 8 1 8 ...
...
```

Now build a new number. Look at the first digit after the decimal of the first number — it is 3. Change it to anything else, say 4. Look at the second digit of the second number — it is 1. Change it to 2. Look at the third digit of the third number — it is 0. Change it to 1. Keep going, taking the diagonal and changing each digit.

Your new number differs from the first number in the first digit. It differs from the second number in the second digit. It differs from the third number in the third digit. It differs from every number on the list in at least one digit, which means it is not on the list. But it is a perfectly valid decimal between 0 and 1. So the list was incomplete.

This works no matter what list you construct. Therefore no complete list exists. The real numbers between 0 and 1 are a larger infinity than the counting numbers.

Cantor called these different sizes of infinity "cardinalities." The counting numbers have cardinality ℵ₀ (aleph-null — pronounced aleph-zero). The real numbers have a larger cardinality, written 𝔠 (for continuum).

This was deeply disturbing to many mathematicians at the time. It is foundational to everything that follows.

### The Axiom of Choice

Sets become genuinely dangerous when you ask the following question: if you have infinitely many sets, each containing at least one element, can you always pick one element from each?

This seems obvious. Of course you can pick one from each. But when the sets are infinite in number and you have no rule for which element to pick, proving you can make such selections turns out to require a new axiom — something you add to your foundation of mathematics as a starting assumption rather than proving from anything else.

This axiom is called the Axiom of Choice, and it says: yes, you can always make such selections, even when infinitely many choices are required and no rule specifies how to make them.

The Axiom of Choice seems obviously true. It also leads directly to the Banach-Tarski theorem. This is not a coincidence.

Here is a way to feel the strangeness. Imagine infinitely many pairs of shoes — left shoes and right shoes. To pick one shoe from each pair, you can use a rule: always pick the left one. Now imagine infinitely many pairs of identical socks — indistinguishable from each other. There is no rule to follow. To pick one sock from each pair, you need the Axiom of Choice to guarantee the selection is even possible.

Most mathematicians accept the Axiom of Choice. Some do not. The Banach-Tarski theorem depends on it. In a universe without the Axiom of Choice, the theorem cannot be proven — and may not hold.

### Measuring Things: Lebesgue Measure

When you want to measure the size of a set of real numbers, you use something called a measure. The standard one is the Lebesgue measure, named after Henri Lebesgue who developed it in the early 1900s.

For an interval of real numbers — say all the numbers between 0 and 1 — the Lebesgue measure is its length: 1. For an interval from 0 to 5, the measure is 5. For a two-dimensional region, the measure is its area. For a three-dimensional region, it is its volume.

The Lebesgue measure has properties that match our physical intuition:

**Countable additivity.** If you split a set into pieces that do not overlap, the total measure equals the sum of the measures of the pieces. A ball with volume 1 cut into pieces whose volumes add up to 1.

**Translation invariance.** Moving a set does not change its measure. A ball in one location has the same volume as the same ball moved across the room.

**Rotation invariance.** Rotating a set does not change its measure. A ball rotated to a different orientation is still the same volume.

These properties are so natural that we rarely think about them. They are the mathematical encoding of the intuition that you cannot create or destroy volume by rearranging things.

The Banach-Tarski theorem does not violate these properties. It does something more subtle: it uses pieces whose measure is simply undefined. You cannot apply the rules to the pieces because the rules do not apply. The pieces are non-measurable sets.

---

### A First Example: The Vitali Set

Before Banach and Tarski, a mathematician named Giuseppe Vitali showed in 1905 that non-measurable sets exist. Here is the construction.

Consider all the real numbers between 0 and 1. Now define two numbers to be "equivalent" if their difference is a rational number — a fraction like 1/3 or 17/100. For example, 0.5 and 0.75 are equivalent because their difference is 0.25, which is 1/4, a rational number. The number π/4 (roughly 0.785) and π/4 + 1/3 are equivalent because their difference is 1/3.

This equivalence relation divides all the numbers in [0,1] into classes. Each class contains all the numbers that are rational distances apart from each other.

Now, using the Axiom of Choice, pick exactly one number from each class. Call the resulting set V. This set V is the Vitali set.

Here is the problem. You can show that the interval [0,1] can be covered by taking V and shifting it by different rational numbers. The shifted copies of V do not overlap, and they tile the interval (with some careful handling of the endpoints, which do not matter for the argument).

If V had a well-defined measure — call it m — then all the shifted copies would also have measure m (by translation invariance), and because they are countably many copies that tile [0,1], the total would have to equal 1 (the measure of [0,1]).

But countably many copies of the same number summing to 1 is impossible. If m = 0, the sum is 0, not 1. If m > 0, the sum is infinite, not 1. There is no value of m that works. Therefore m cannot be defined. The Vitali set has no measure.

This is the first non-measurable set. It does not look like anything physical. It is not a weird shape. It is a perfectly well-defined collection of real numbers that simply breaks the machinery of measurement.

The key ingredient was the Axiom of Choice — it is what allowed picking one element from each equivalence class without any rule for which element to pick. Without the Axiom of Choice, the argument does not go through.

A non-measurable set is a collection of points that has no well-defined size.

This is not the same as having size zero, or infinite size. It means the question "how big is this?" has no answer. The set exists. Its points are perfectly legitimate points. You can describe membership in it precisely. But if you try to assign it a volume — or a length, or an area — the answer you get depends on how you ask the question, and the different ways of asking give different answers.

Physical intuition has no category for this. Every physical object has a size. The non-measurable set is a mathematical object that exists outside the reach of measurement.

This is not a contradiction. It is a feature of what happens when you allow the full power of infinite choice. The Axiom of Choice lets you construct collections of points so finely irregular that no consistent notion of size can be assigned to them.

---

## Part Three: Groups, Rotations, and Free Groups

### What Is a Group?

A group is a set of operations with specific properties. The operations can be composed — you can do one after another. Every operation has an inverse — something that undoes it. There is an identity operation — one that does nothing. And the operations are associative — it does not matter how you group them when composing several at once.

The rotations of a sphere form a group. You can rotate by any angle around any axis. You can do two rotations in sequence. Every rotation has an inverse rotation that puts things back. The identity rotation does nothing. And for three or more rotations in sequence, it does not matter how you parenthesize them.

### The Free Group on Two Generators

Consider a group with exactly two operations, which we will call A and B. And their inverses, which we call A⁻¹ and B⁻¹.

In the free group on two generators, the only simplification rule is that A and A⁻¹ cancel each other out (and similarly B and B⁻¹). Otherwise, every sequence of operations is distinct.

So the elements of this group are all finite sequences, or words, built from A, B, A⁻¹, B⁻¹, without consecutive cancellations:

Identity (the empty word), A, B, A⁻¹, B⁻¹, AA, AB, AA⁻¹ (this simplifies to identity), AB⁻¹, BA, BB, ...

The free group is infinite. Its elements grow exponentially with word length: 4 words of length 1, 12 words of length 2 (since you cannot immediately cancel), and so on.

The crucial property is this: the free group can be split into pieces that reassemble into two copies of itself. This is the algebraic heart of the Banach-Tarski paradox.

Here is how. Let W(A) be all words that start with A. Let W(A⁻¹) be all words starting with A⁻¹. Similarly W(B) and W(B⁻¹). Add in the identity.

Notice that the whole group equals W(A) ∪ A⁻¹·W(A) — meaning everything starting with A, plus the identity prepended to everything starting with A, after applying A⁻¹. Why? Because prepending A⁻¹ to every word in W(A) gives you every word starting with A⁻¹ or the identity. So W(A) together with A⁻¹W(A) covers the whole group.

Similarly W(B) ∪ B⁻¹·W(B) covers the whole group.

So the group can be split into W(A), W(A⁻¹), W(B), W(B⁻¹), and {identity} — and from these pieces, just by shifting them (applying one generator), you can reassemble two complete copies of the group.

This is the abstract algebraic structure that the paradox will transfer to the sphere.

The rotation group SO(3) contains every rotation of the three-dimensional sphere. The key fact, proved by Hausdorff, is that SO(3) contains a copy of the free group on two generators.

Specifically, there exist two rotations — call them φ and ψ — such that the only relations between them are the ones forced by them being inverses of each other. No sequence of these two rotations and their inverses, other than obvious cancellations, equals the identity.

This is done by careful analysis of what these rotations do to specific points, using a clever encoding that tracks whether particular coordinates remain rational.

The key result: these two rotations generate an infinite group isomorphic to the free group — the same structure we just described.

- A is congruent to B (one can be rotated to become the other)
- A is congruent to C
- A is congruent to B ∪ C (A can be rotated to become the union of B and C)

This is already strange. One piece is congruent to itself joined with another piece. A is the same "size" as A together with B — which would mean B has no size, or that size does not work the way we think.

The construction uses the free group sitting inside SO(3). The sphere minus the countable set of "bad" poles is acted on by this group, and the free group's paradoxical decomposition transfers to the sphere.

The countable set excluded is the set of all points that are fixed by some non-identity rotation in our free group — the poles of each rotation.
